description: Team AETHERIA is a solo team. I am a 7th grade student who loves space, astronauts and NASA missions. For this challenge I built "Lunar Base Mission Trainer", a 3D Unity game where kids travel from a NASA base on Earth to the Moon's south pole and run a lunar outpost for 30 days using real NASA data (DONKI solar storms, radiation limits, life support values). I work with Unity, C# and Python, and I am learning game design, level building and 3D modeling.
summary: Lunar Base Mission Trainer is a Unity game for kids aged 7–12 that turns the real engineering trade-offs of a lunar outpost into hands-on decisions. The player starts at a NASA base on Earth, wires the shuttle, chooses limited cargo (every kilogram costs fuel), launches, lands at the Moon's south pole and then runs a base for 30 lunar days. They must balance life support (an O₂ filter procedure based on NASA BVAD values), radiation shielding (a shelter and regolith sandbags during solar storms pulled live from NASA's DONKI API), power through the 14.75-day lunar night, food production in a greenhouse that has to be diagnosed, and communication delay with Mission Control. A 3D drone flight into a shadowed crater shows why the water ice found by LCROSS matters. Every task trains a thinking skill (planning, prioritizing, cause and effect, following procedures, diagnosis and risk management), and the end-of-mission report shows the child's decisions together with the NASA sources behind every number. The game runs on keyboard and mouse, and the drone can optionally be flown with hand gestures through a webcam.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lunar Base Mission Trainer is a Unity game for kids aged 7–12 that answers the challenge's call to show the real engineering trade-offs of a lunar mission at a level a young learner can handle. The child plays a trainee astronaut on one continuous journey: preparing a shuttle at a NASA base on Earth, choosing cargo, launching, landing at the Moon's south pole and running an outpost for 30 lunar days (about 10 minutes of play).

HOW IT WORKS

1) Earth base: move the shuttle to the pad on the crawler and wire 4 cockpit cables correctly (controls tutorial).

2) Cargo choice: 6 options but only 3 slots (extra battery, extra solar panel, water-wall shelter, extra food, advanced science kit, a 2-slot fission reactor). Every kilogram costs fuel (F = m·a), and the choice changes how the Moon mission plays out.

3) Launch, trans-lunar injection and a cinematic landing at the south pole, where Earth sits low on the horizon.

4) Moon base, with a different kind of task in every module: Habitat (life support) – switch systems at the power panel and replace a clogged O₂ filter with a 5-step procedure where every step explains why. Greenhouse (food) – read light, water, CO₂ and temperature sensors, find the faulty one and pick the right repair. Shelter (radiation) – take cover when a solar storm hits and carry regolith sandbags to halve the storm dose. Antenna (communication) – ask Mission Control and wait out the 1.3 s + 1.3 s light delay; contact is lost when Earth sets. Solar panels (power) – repair meteor damage and carry a 20 kg battery cell by drone before the 14.75-day lunar night. Drone station (science) – fly a 3D drone into a permanently shadowed crater to collect water-ice samples; the battery drains with speed and the drone is lost if it runs out.

5) End-of-mission report: stars, radiation dose taken, procedure mistakes, science points and the list of every NASA source used (also available in-game with the K key).

REAL NASA DATA

Solar flares of the last 30 days are pulled live from the NASA DONKI API and become in-game storms; offline, real archived events (X8.7 14 May 2024, X9.0 3 Oct 2024, X8.2 10 Sep 2017, August 1972) are used and clearly labeled ARCHIVE. Radiation uses the 600 mSv career limit from NASA-STD-3001 and the lunar surface dose measured by Chang'e-4 (1.369 mSv/day). Oxygen use follows NASA BVAD (0.82 kg O₂ per person per day). The crater task is based on LCROSS and LRO Diviner results, the greenhouse on NASA Veggie, the fission cargo on NASA's Fission Surface Power project, and the storm dose comparison on Curiosity RAD data from May 2024. Values scaled to fit 10 minutes are marked in-game.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Each task trains a thinking skill rather than reflexes: planning (cargo), prioritizing (power before night), cause and effect (night = no solar + more heating), following procedures (filter change), diagnosis (greenhouse sensors) and risk management (storm warning: finish the task or take shelter?). Because the numbers are real, children learn why astronauts plan, wait for Mission Control and build shelters, and teachers can connect the game to physics (F = m·a, speed of light) and biology (plants, radiation).

CREATIVITY

The whole mission is one continuous story from Earth to the Moon; real space weather of the current month appears in the game; communication delay is something the child feels, not just reads (a delayed drone-control mode); and an optional webcam hand-gesture mode (Python + MediaPipe, 21 hand points, UDP to Unity) lets kids fly the drone with an open hand, fist and pinch. Everything also works with keyboard and mouse so every child can play.

TOOLS

Unity 6 (C#, URP, Input System), Python, OpenCV, MediaPipe, NASA Open APIs (DONKI), Blender, NASA 3D Resources (Space Shuttle model), Poly Haven textures. Windows build, source code and presentations: https://github.com/ahmetcinaraksoy07-cell/AETHERIA-Lunar-Base-Mission-Trainer
